title: China adds AI agent checks before phones, tablets and wearables can go on sale
excerpt: China's industry ministry says devices with a built-in AI agent must pass compatibility and anti-fraud checks, and agents should carry a unique identity code.

sources.title: China Sourcing Post: China requires AI-agent checks in network-access approval for phones, tablets and wearables
Compsmag: China's MIIT brings AI-agent smartphones, tablets and wearables under new network-access rules
Ctrl+AI+Reg newsletter: "Passports for bots": China's gameplan to control AI agent identity (9 November 2026)

body_html:
China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) has published new rules for phones, tablets, wearables and other telecom devices that come with an AI agent already installed. The notice, numbered 42 of 2026, was posted on the ministry's website on 6 November 2026.

In China, phones and similar devices need a network-access licence before they can be connected to public networks and sold. The new notice brings AI agents into that licensing process. MIIT describes an agent as an AI system that can perceive, remember, decide, interact and carry out tasks on its own.

What the notice asks for

According to reports on the notice, the main requirements are:

  • Compatibility checks: agent developers must verify that their agent works safely with each device model and operating system. The checks cover how the agent uses permissions, communications, network and data security, user rights and how it carries out tasks.
  • Anti-fraud testing: devices with a built-in agent must undergo a fraud-risk assessment and an anti-fraud capability test as part of network-access testing.
  • An identity code: agents on a device should carry a unique identity code, linked to China's national standards on how agents connect to each other.
  • No forced access to other apps: app stores must let app developers declare whether they allow agents to operate their app. Without that consent, an agent may not force its way into the app.
  • Control over updates: before a major over-the-air update to an agent, makers must file a plan with the ministry, including network, data and anti-fraud measures. The new service can be offered only after an expert review.
  • Same product as tested: the device sold must match the one that was tested, and major changes must be reported.

Reports say the ministry presents the aim as keeping AI under human control while letting development continue.

What is still unclear

The reports do not give a separate start date or a transition period for devices already on the market. They also do not explain exactly how the anti-fraud assessment will be carried out, which test standards apply, or whether devices made only for export are covered. We were not able to open the ministry's own notice, so this story relies on published summaries of it.

Why it matters for staying in charge

An AI agent on a phone can open apps, send messages and make payments for its owner. That is useful, and it is also a new way for things to go wrong if the agent is misused or tricked. China's approach puts three ideas in place before devices reach people.

First, an agent should be identifiable, so a bank, an app or a person can tell when they are dealing with software rather than a human (D4 Honest identity). Second, an agent should only reach what it has been allowed to reach. The rule that agents cannot force their way into apps without consent is a clear example of bounded autonomy (D2 Bounded autonomy). Third, security and fraud protection are checked before sale and again when the agent is updated (D6 Secure and supported, D10 Safe for its whole life).

Wherever you live, it is worth asking any maker of a device with a built-in assistant what it can do on its own, how you can limit it and how you can turn it off. Our Questions to ask page has more.
